## Confounders, mediators and colliders {#dag-crash-course-three-roles .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: mini-dags
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
# Three tiny DAGs: confounder / mediator / collider. Each arrow is an R formula
# read outcome-first, so `X ~ Z` is the arrow Z -> X; dagify() takes the
# coordinates, the exposure and the outcome in the same call, and returns a
# plain dagitty object that adjustmentSets() and paths() accept unchanged.
conf <- ggdag::dagify(X ~ Z, Y ~ X + Z,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, Z = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 1)))
med  <- ggdag::dagify(M ~ X, Y ~ M + X,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, M = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, M = 1)))
coll <- ggdag::dagify(C ~ X + Y, Y ~ X,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, C = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, C = -1)))

# Edges are coloured by role: the X -> Y causal effect (the estimand) is GREEN
# in every panel; the secondary structure is drawn in an accent – RED where it
# biases the naive estimate (the confounder fork, the collider edges) and AMBER
# for the indirect path through the mediator, which is part of the total effect
# rather than bias. The accent is passed per panel; green is constant so the eye
# learns 'green = the effect I want, coloured = the path I must reason about'.
gg <- function(d, ttl, cap, accent = d_red) {
  td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(d)
  ggdag::update_dag_data(td) <- dplyr::mutate(ggdag::pull_dag_data(td),
    edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "causal", "other"))
  ggplot2::ggplot(td,
      ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
      arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"),
                                   type = "closed")) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 16, colour = "black") +
    ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4) +
    ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
      values = c(causal = green, other = accent), guide = "none") +
    ggdag::theme_dag() +
    # Expand the panel so the nodes sit well inside it – otherwise the title
    # and caption crowd (and slightly cover) the top/bottom nodes.
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.32)) +
    ggplot2::labs(title = ttl, caption = cap) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                                hjust = 0.5, size = 16,
                                margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11,
                                  colour = grey_mid, lineheight = 1.05,
                                  margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 10)))
}
  patchwork::wrap_plots(
    gg(conf, "Confounder Z",
       "Common cause of X and Y.\nADJUST – or the estimate is biased.", d_red),
    gg(med,  "Mediator M",
       "Lies on the path X → Y.\nDON'T adjust if you want the total effect.", orange),
    gg(coll, "Collider C",
       "Caused by both X and Y.\nNEVER adjust – it opens a spurious path.", d_red),
    nrow = 1)
```

::: {.src}
X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.
:::

::: notes
The causal graph serves the second of those steps, and these three small graphs cover all the theory of graphs that the tasks need. In every panel the green arrow is the effect of X on Y that you are after, and what changes is the coloured structure around it. A confounder is a common cause of predictor and outcome, and its red fork is a back-door path, which biases the estimate while it stays open, so you adjust for the confounder to close it. A mediator lies on the causal path between the two, and since the amber path is part of the total effect, you do not adjust for the mediator if the total effect is what you want. A collider is caused by both sides, and its edges are harmless until you condition on it, which opens a spurious path. The rules are short: adjust for confounders, leave mediators alone for a total effect, and never condition on a collider.
:::

## Causal stories behind a correlation {#one-number-many-stories .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}

```{r}
#| label: many-stories
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.3
# A single strong association. The same slope is consistent with several
# different causal structures – the number alone cannot tell you which one
# generated it (the 'causal quartet' point). Scatter is simulated for display.
set.seed(11)
n <- 130; x <- rnorm(n); y <- 0.6 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.85)
df <- tibble::tibble(x, y)
ggplot2::ggplot(df, ggplot2::aes(x, y)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = ncl_blue, alpha = 0.5, size = 2.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = d_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = min(x), y = max(y), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           label = paste0("r = ", format(round(cor(x, y), 2), nsmall = 2)),
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 6.5) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "X", y = "Y") + theme_slide(16)
```

:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.small}
The same slope fits four different stories:

::: {.fragment}
- X really causes Y – the slope *is* the effect
:::
::: {.fragment}
- a common cause inflates it – **confounding**
:::
::: {.fragment}
- the sample itself is selected – **collider / selection**
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Y causes X (**reverse causation**), or it is **chance**
:::
::: {.fragment}
The data look identical in all four. Only an assumption about *how the data arose* can tell them apart, and a DAG is where you write that assumption down.
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot; @KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated. Scatter simulated for illustration.
:::

::: notes
The scatter shows a strong correlation, an r of about nought point six, and before you reach for a model, consider that this one number is consistent with at least four stories. [advance] X may really cause Y, so that the slope is the effect. [advance] A common cause may inflate it. [advance] The sample may be selected, so that the association is an artefact of who got in. [advance] Or Y may cause X, or the association may be chance. [advance] Nothing in the data can decide between these stories, because the scatter looks the same in every case, and only an assumption about how the data were generated can do so. A DAG is where you write that assumption down, which is why we draw one before we fit anything.
:::

## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: backdoor-paths
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 3.7
# Same confounder graph, twice. LEFT: the back-door path X <- Z -> Y is open
# (red), so the naive X -> Y estimate is biased. RIGHT: adjusting for Z (boxed)
# blocks the back-door (greyed), leaving the green causal path clean. Reuses
# `conf` from the mini-dags chunk.
path_panel <- function(adjust_z = FALSE) {
  td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(conf)
  ggdag::update_dag_data(td) <- dplyr::mutate(ggdag::pull_dag_data(td),
    edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "causal",
                       if (adjust_z) "blocked" else "backdoor"))
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(td,
      ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
      arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"),
                                   type = "closed")) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 18, colour = "black") +
    ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4.4) +
    ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
      values = c(causal = green, backdoor = d_red, blocked = grey_mid),
      guide = "none") +
    ggdag::theme_dag() +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.22)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.40)) +
    ggplot2::labs(title = if (adjust_z) "Adjust for Z → back-door closed"
                          else "Back-door path X ← Z → Y is open") +
    ggplot2::theme(plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                                hjust = 0.5, size = 15, margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 8)))
  if (adjust_z) {
    zc <- datawizard::data_filter(ggdag::pull_dag_data(td), name == "Z")[1, ]
    p <- p + ggplot2::annotate("point", x = zc$x, y = zc$y, shape = 0,
                               size = 14, stroke = 1.6, colour = ncl_blue)
  }
  p
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(path_panel(FALSE), path_panel(TRUE), nrow = 1)
```

::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust for the variable in its middle. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened when you adjust for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.
:::

::: notes
A DAG is read through its paths. Association flows along every open path between X and Y, not only along the causal arrow, so the job is to work out which paths are open and to close the ones that you do not want. Two rules do all the work. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting for the variable in the middle, as with the red back-door fork on the left, whereas a path through a collider is closed by default and opened by adjustment. The back-door criterion combines the two rules: close every path that enters X from behind, and leave the causal path from X to Y open. Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading of the estimate.
:::

## Total effect or direct effect {#which-effect-do-you-even-want .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: total-direct
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.1
# Mediator graph with the two routes coloured: the DIRECT effect X -> Y (green)
# and the INDIRECT route X -> M -> Y (amber). Together they make the total
# effect; adjusting for M leaves only the direct one. Reuses `med`.
td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(med)
ggdag::update_dag_data(td) <- dplyr::mutate(ggdag::pull_dag_data(td),
  edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "direct", "indirect"))
ggplot2::ggplot(td,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(8, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 22, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 5) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c(direct = green, indirect = orange),
    guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.30)) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = "indirect", colour = orange,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5, angle = 33) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.14, label = "direct", colour = green,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5)
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
- **Total** = direct (green) + indirect (amber)
- Adjust for the mediator M → you estimate the **direct** effect only – a *different* estimand
- 'Control for everything' can switch you to an estimand you never chose
- **Table 2 fallacy**: the other coefficients in your model are *not* all causal effects
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated; @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot.
:::

::: notes
Suppose that M lies between your predictor and your outcome. The total effect is the green arrow plus the amber route through M, and the direct effect is the green arrow alone. These are different numbers answering different questions, and which one you obtain depends on whether M is in the model, so that a mediator added as one more 'control' switches the estimate to the direct effect without anyone noticing, the analyst included. This is why 'control for everything' is poor advice. A corollary is the Table 2 fallacy: in a printed regression table usually only one coefficient has a clean causal reading, and the coefficients of the control variables are not causal effects of their own.
:::

## Selection and feedback {#spurious-by-design-selection-feedback .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: selection-panel
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.7
# LEFT: a collider S caused by A and B. Conditioning on (or sampling on) S –
# the red box – induces a spurious A–B association (dashed red). RIGHT: a
# two-wave cross-lagged panel. The claim U1 -> F2 is green; the reverse path
# F1 -> U2 is red; the autoregressive paths are grey. Two-way FE handles
# neither feedback nor time-varying confounding.
sel <- ggdag::dagify(S ~ A + B,
  coords = list(x = c(A = 0, S = 1, B = 2), y = c(A = 0, S = 1, B = 0)))
tds <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(sel)
ggdag::update_dag_data(tds) <- dplyr::mutate(ggdag::pull_dag_data(tds), edge_kind = "structural")
p_sel <- ggplot2::ggplot(tds,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 18, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4.4) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c(structural = grey_mid), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::annotate("point", x = 1, y = 1, shape = 0, size = 14, stroke = 1.6,
                    colour = d_red) +
  ggplot2::annotate("curve", x = 0.12, y = -0.18, xend = 1.88, yend = -0.18,
    curvature = -0.25, colour = d_red, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(6, "pt"), ends = "both")) +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.22)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.45)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Condition on collider S → spurious A–B link") +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                              hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 8)))

clp <- ggdag::dagify(U2 ~ U1 + F1, F2 ~ F1 + U1,
  coords = list(x = c(U1 = 0, F1 = 0, U2 = 2, F2 = 2),
                y = c(U1 = 1, F1 = 0, U2 = 1, F2 = 0)))
tdc <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(clp)
ggdag::update_dag_data(tdc) <- dplyr::mutate(ggdag::pull_dag_data(tdc), edge_kind = dplyr::case_when(
  name == "U1" & to == "F2" ~ "claim",
  name == "F1" & to == "U2" ~ "reverse",
  TRUE ~ "auto"))
p_clp <- ggplot2::ggplot(tdc,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 20, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 3.6) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
    values = c(claim = green, reverse = d_red, auto = grey_mid), guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.30)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Panel feedback: U now → F later, but also F → U") +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                              hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = ggplot2::margin(b = 8)))
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_sel, p_clp, nrow = 1)
```

::: {.small}
- **Selection / collider bias** – conditioning, or merely *sampling*, on a common effect manufactures an association that was never there (much of the early COVID risk-factor literature)
- **Reverse causation & feedback** – in a panel, today's outcome can move tomorrow's predictor; two-way fixed effects absorb stable country traits and common-year shocks, **not** time-varying feedback (U = unemployment, F = framing)
:::

::: {.src}
@GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines; @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue; @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse.
:::

::: notes
Two last ways in which a relationship can be spurious both apply to our case study. The first is selection, or collider bias: conditioning on, or merely sampling on, something that both variables cause produces a correlation out of nothing, as in much of the early research on risk factors for COVID, which drew on people who had been tested, a selected group. The second is reverse causation and feedback. Our data are a panel, in which today's outcome can feed tomorrow's predictor. Two-way fixed effects, the baseline design for our claim, absorb stable differences between countries and shocks common to a year, but they do not on their own deal with a time-varying confounder or a feedback loop, which matters when we build the graph for our own paper.
:::
